new_statements.quote: Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not. Distinctive vowel length may occur between any vowel other than the final vowel of a word and a single consonant; e.g. Leg sa:lug 'river' (cf. salug 'floor'); ma:ba:sa 'will read' (cf. maba:sa 'able to be read'). Length is non-distinctive after the final vowel of a word. In inherited words, length does not occur before a consonant cluster. [p. 51] ... Basic vowel length within a root is fixed arbitrarily in the lexicon. That is, in its basic lexical form, a root has either a long or short penultimate vowel. Thus there are minimal pairs such as Leg salug 'floor', sa:lug 'river'. [p. 61]
new_statements.citation: McFarland, Curtis Daniel. 1974. The dialects of the Bikol area. PhD dissertation, Yale University (Xerox University Microfilms 75-15,337).
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 (phonology), p. 51 (PDF p. 43) and p. 61 (PDF p. 53); text layer is ABBYY scanned of a microfilm scan
new_statements.rule_in_words: No distinctive stress in the sense of loudness; instead every root carries a lexically arbitrary long or short penultimate vowel (the Philippine accent contrast), so accent placement is unpredictable from the segmental shape and must be listed per root; suffixation shifts the length rightward and some affixes impose penult length.
new_statements.exceptions: Length occurs before consonant clusters only in loans (pi:dru, gu:stu); length after the final vowel of a word is non-distinctive; lexically fixed length shifts under suffixation (p. 61-62). Lobel 2013: fn. 3 p. 287 warns that some Bikol subgroup members have lost contrastive stress (Lobel 2003 on Rinconada), so individual Inland varieties may differ; Olson et al. 2009's Buhi'non list shows mostly final stress in citation forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/lexical forms; the statement is made once for 'all Bikol area dialects' (the eleven dialects surveyed, including the Inland dialects Daraga, Oas, Libon and Buhi that make up alba1269), and the illustrative forms are Legazpi (Coastal Bikol). McFarland explicitly denies distinctive stress (loudness) and locates the contrast in vowel length; this is the ordinary Philippine 'accent' contrast (long penult = penult accent vs short penult = final accent), which is why the reading is lexical-unpredictable rather than no-word-stress-per-source. Morphophonemics: with most verbal suffixes the length moves to the root-final vowel (basa:hun); certain affixes impose penult length regardless of the root (paraqu:ma, paraba:sa); length never precedes a consonant cluster in inherited words.
new_statements.identity_note: McFarland 1974 is a survey of eleven Bikol-area dialects; the deciding statement is made for 'all Bikol area dialects' and the examples are Legazpi (Coastal Bikol, cent2087). Of his Inland dialects, Daraga and Oas (= Miraya/West Albay), Libon and Buhi belong to alba1269, while Iriga is Rinconada (irig1242). No opened source gives a stress rule for one alba1269 variety alone; the Buhi'non wordlist (Olson et al. 2009, Buhi, Camarines Sur; ABVD glottocode buhi1243) is corpus evidence only. Wikipedia's claim that Albay Bikol 'lacks stressed syllables' is unsourced and contradicted by the wordlist and Lobel 2005 accent marks. Fincke 2002 (Sto. Domingo, Albay) is linked by Glottolog to alba1269 but Sto. Domingo is a coastal town, so that link is doubtful.

sources.locator: Chapter 2 (phonology), p. 51 (PDF p. 43) and p. 61 (PDF p. 53); text layer is ABBYY scanned of a microfilm scan
sources.note: Ch. 2 phonology, p. 51 (PDF p. 43): 'Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not'; length contrasts only on a non-final vowel before a single consonant; p. 61-62: basic vowel length is fixed arbitrarily in the lexicon (long vs short penult, minimal pairs salug/sa:lug) and shifts under suffixation (basa:hun, paraqu:ma). Covers the Inland dialects Daraga, Oas, Libon, Buhi (all alba1269) plus Iriga, Coastal, Catanduanes and Southern dialects; examples are Legazpi.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/101972
sources.note: No phonology of Inland Bikol; fn. 3 p. 287: 'It is not at all uncommon for one or more members of a Philippine subgroup to have lost contrastive stress while others retain it, as this is exactly what has happened both in the Bikol subgroup (Lobel 2003) and the Cordilleran subgroup (Zorc 1979).' Buhi-non, Libon, Miraya data appear only in pronoun/lexical tables.

sources.citation: Olson, Kenneth S., Emy T. Ballenas & Nilo M. Borromeo. 2009. Buhi'non (Bikol) digital wordlist: Presentation form. Language Documentation & Conservation 3(2): 213-225. http://hdl.handle.net/10125/4440
sources.note: No prose statement on stress; the 207-item IPA wordlist marks stress on every item (e.g. [ʔaˈko] 'I', [kaˈmo] 'you pl.', [baˈto] 'stone', [ʔadˈto] 'there', [ŋaˈran] 'name'; penult in [ʔamwaˈdi]/[piˈra]-type forms), i.e. a corpus in which stress is mostly final in citation forms. Notes only the extra phonemes /ɣ/ and /ə/.

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2005. The angry register of the Bikol languages of the Philippines. In Hsiu-chuan Liao & Carl Rubino (eds.), Current issues in Philippine linguistics and anthropology: Parangal kay Lawrence A. Reid, 149-166. Manila: LSP & SIL.
sources.note: Marks each Buhi-non/Libon/Oas angry-register item as 'pp.' (penult stress) or 'pc.' (ultima stress) -- i.e. treats accent placement as lexical in these varieties -- but gives no rule.
